about: Daily Synopsis: the fixed lists the check (daily-synopsis/lib/check.mjs) refuses a model's draft by. Each entry is matched as a whole word or phrase, ignoring case and accents, after curly apostrophes are made straight. An entry ending in * stands for the word and every longer word that begins so (ignor* is ignore, ignored, ignoring and ignorant). An entry with … between its words allows up to six words in the gap (described … as is also described the summit as), the first of them not for, on, off, up, in, out or back. tests/daily-synopsis.test.mjs tests every entry, and daily-synopsis/scripts/prompt-lists.mjs writes them into PROMPT.md. Edit only with a test, and run prompt-lists.mjs after.

reportedSpeech.about: Words that mark a sentence as someone's words (reported speech). Refused in every sentence of the digest and of the 5 Sided Analysis.

judgement.about: Words and phrases that state a motive, an intent or a judgement of a side or an outlet. Refused in the written 5 Sided Analysis: it says what the headlines put first, never why. Besides this list, a side's sentence may not go on after the word first with to and a verb (first to stir fear): that too gives a purpose.

judgementEverywhere.about: The part of the judgement list refused in every sentence, the digest's own included: words that call something biased or a lie. In the digest a word is allowed when a headline or summary the sentence cites has the same word (a law on propaganda, a study of bias); in the 5 Sided Analysis never.

journalist.about: Words that name a journalist's or a publisher's role. Refused in the written 5 Sided Analysis, where outlets appear only as linked headlines, never in VM's prose.

outlets.about: Publishers' names besides the Political Briefing's own catalogue (whose names the check reads from briefing/scripts/sources.mjs). Refused in every sentence of the digest and of the 5 Sided Analysis, in any case, except the names in outletCommonWords, which are refused only with their capitals.

outletCommonWords.about: Outlets' names that are also ordinary English words (a fox, a slate of candidates, a blaze, the nation). Each is refused as an outlet only when written with its capital, as a name; every other outlet's name is refused in any case (bbc, the guardian).

instructionLike.about: Phrases that read as an instruction to a reader or a model rather than a description of the news. Refused in every sentence.

closingSame.about: The words of difference. A closing sentence of kind same may not hold one: the page shows it after Left and right of centre alike, so it may not say that they differ. A closing sentence of kind differ must hold one.

closingDiffer.about: The words of sameness. A closing sentence of kind differ may not hold one: the page shows it after Left and right of centre, as a difference, so it may not say that they are alike. A closing sentence of kind same must hold one (no difference and not differ count as sameness, not as difference).

dateNames.about: Months and weekdays. Written with a capital, they are names, and like any name must be in the text of the items the sentence cites, and printed by two outlets; one that is not is refused as a date. The full names, and may, are dates in lower case too: may, the verb, must be in the items the sentence cites like any other word.

relativeDates.about: Date words written in lower case. Like a month, a weekday or a year, each must be in the text of the items the sentence cites (a plural counts as its singular).

numberWords.about: Numbers written as words. Each must be in the text of the items the sentence cites, as the word or as its figure. (Not first or half, which headlines and the 5 Sided Analysis use in other senses: what a headline puts first. Like every other word, first and half must still be in the items cited, but for first after put or puts: see supportWords.)

supportWords.about: The support rule: every word of every sentence must be in the headline or summary of an item the sentence cites (exactly, or as another form of it: plural -s or -es, -ies for -y, -ed, -ied, -d or -ing), or be one of these. A closed list of words that carry no fact of their own: articles, the plainer prepositions and conjunctions, pronouns, the forms of be, have and do, and the few neutral words a 5 Sided Analysis needs to describe coverage. It holds no number word, no month or weekday, no verb of saying, no word of judgement or motive and no word that gives an order; and on purpose not not, no, never, against, without, up, down, off, out, nor any modal verb (will, may, could, should). Besides these, first counts as supported in the same clause after put, puts or putting (what a headline puts first).

openers.about: Words a sentence may begin with although they are not in its items: the first word of a sentence is capitalised, and when it is one of these it is not taken for a name. A first word that the day's headlines and summaries also print in lower case (Federal, Floods) is not taken for a name either, unless it is in commonWordNames. Every other capitalised word is a name.

commonWordNames.about: Names that are also ordinary English words. A capital at the start of a headline or a summary's sentence, or in a headline written in title case, says nothing about whether such a word is a name there, so it is not taken as a second outlet printing the name: a private person called Hope is not carried because another outlet's headline begins Hope fades.
